titre: Montesquieu Describes an England He Does Not Claim to Have Verified
accroche: In 1748, Montesquieu builds the separation of powers on England. In the same chapter, he warns that he has not checked whether the law is actually applied.
contenu_vulgarise:
1748. Montesquieu publishes *De l'esprit des lois* (*The Spirit of Laws*), a work that d'Alembert says had been pondered for twenty years. The author had spent eighteen months in England, from November 1729 to the spring of 1731. Chapter 6 of Book XI, “Of the Constitution of England,” has become one of the founding texts of constitutional law: it is the source of the idea that political liberty requires separating powers.

## Three Powers, One Condition

Montesquieu distinguishes three powers in every state: the legislative power, the executive power over matters that depend on the law of nations (the executive, in the modern sense), and the executive power over matters that depend on civil law (the power of judging). His formula fits in a single sentence: when the legislative and executive powers are united in the same hand, there is no liberty, because one may fear that the same monarch or the same senate will make tyrannical laws in order to execute them tyrannically. The same is true if the power of judging is not separated from either of the other two. In the English Constitution as he presents it, the legislative body is made up of two parts, and each chains the other by their mutual faculty of rejecting; both are bound by the executive power, which is itself bound by the legislative.

## A Sentence Almost No One Reads

Near the end of the chapter, long after this theory that became a commonplace of political thought, Montesquieu writes a sentence that posterity has largely set aside: “It is not for me to examine whether the English actually enjoy this liberty or not. It is enough for me to say that it is established by their laws, and I seek no further.” In other words, he does not claim to have verified that the England of 1748 really works as he has just described. He describes what the laws establish, not a field observation, for anyone willing to read the chapter to the end.

That does not mean he did not know the England of his day well: a study chapter from the Presses universitaires d'Aix-Marseille credits him with one of the best understandings of the English political reality of his time. It nonetheless notes that he overlooked certain aspects of the regime, such as local government, and did not dwell on the emergence of the cabinet at the expense of the king's privy council.

What has come down through the centuries is therefore first a principle, more than an account: the work inspired the drafters of the French Constitution of 1791, which keeps the power of judging apart from both the legislative body and the king, and of later constitutions.

citation.texte: It is not for me to examine whether the English actually enjoy this liberty or not. It is enough for me to say that it is established by their laws, and I seek no further.
citation.source: *De l'esprit des lois* (*The Spirit of Laws*), Book XI, chapter 6, 1748 (our translation from the French)

carte.punch: Montesquieu describes English liberty, then writes that he does not examine whether the English enjoy it.
carte.idee: In 1748, Montesquieu builds the separation of powers on the Constitution of England. Near the end of the same chapter, he states that he does not examine whether the English actually enjoy this liberty: he describes what their laws establish.

quiz.question: What does Montesquieu's sentence, “It is not for me to examine whether the English actually enjoy this liberty or not,” reveal?
choix: That he had in fact never set foot in England before writing this chapter.
That he thinks the English of his time enjoy no real political liberty.
That he defers checking this point to a later chapter of the work, which he never actually wrote.
That he presents a theoretical legal model, without claiming to have verified that it matches actual English practice.
quiz.explication: Montesquieu does not say that the English are free or that they are not: he asserts only that their laws establish this liberty, which is not the same as verifying how it is actually applied.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What are the three powers Montesquieu distinguishes in every state?
choix: The royal power, the religious power, and the military power of the state
The legislative power, the executive power over matters of the law of nations, and the power of judging
The legislative power, the media power, and the economic power of the kingdom
The power of the king, that of the lords, and that of the people assembled together
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Montesquieu distinguishes the legislative power, the executive power over matters that depend on the law of nations, and the power of judging, which depends on civil law.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where in chapter 6 does the sentence in which Montesquieu says he does not verify the actual liberty of the English appear?
choix: In the very first sentence of the chapter, before the theory is even laid out
In the preface to the work, before Book XI begins
In a note added by an editor long after Montesquieu's death
Near the end of the chapter, long after the formula on the separation of powers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The sentence comes almost at the end of the chapter, long after the famous formula on the separation of powers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does a study chapter from the Presses universitaires d'Aix-Marseille note about what Montesquieu did not examine in depth in the English system?
choix: The emergence of the ministerial cabinet, which was already taking hold at the expense of the king's privy council
The very existence of a House of Lords distinct from the House of Commons
The English king's ability to veto laws that had been passed
The separation between English civil courts and religious courts
quiz_supplementaire.explication: This chapter notes that he did not dwell on the emergence of the cabinet at the expense of the privy council, while crediting him with a fine understanding of English political reality.
